# Build the Salmon transcriptome index

## Match the index to the workflow mode

For `runall --mode salmon`, `--index` must point to a Salmon transcriptome index directory. Do not supply a STAR genome index, FASTA file, or GTF file.

This tutorial uses the GENCODE human release 36 transcript FASTA:

```text
https://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/gencode/Gencode_human/release_36/
```

GENCODE FASTA headers contain ENST, ENSG, and gene-symbol fields. IOBRpy `prepare_salmon` uses these fields to convert the merged transcript TPM table into a gene symbol × sample matrix.

## Build the index

```bash
bash scripts/build_salmon_index.sh
```

The script creates:

```text
reference/
├── gencode-v36/
│   ├── gencode.v36.transcripts.fa.gz
│   └── gencode.v36.transcripts.fa
└── salmon-gencode-v36/
    ├── versionInfo.json
    └── ...
```

If `versionInfo.json` already exists, the script stops instead of rebuilding the index.

## Check the index

```bash
test -s reference/salmon-gencode-v36/versionInfo.json
python -m json.tool reference/salmon-gencode-v36/versionInfo.json
```

Record the Salmon version:

```bash
salmon --version | tee reference/salmon-version.txt
```

`reference/salmon-version.txt` is a local run record and is excluded from Git by default.

## Why the tutorial does not use a tiny artificial index

A mini-transcriptome containing only a few genes would make Salmon faster, but it would systematically remove most of the expression space required by immune infiltration, signature, and ligand-receptor analyses. The tutorial therefore uses small FASTQ subsets with a complete human transcriptome index.

This is still a teaching run. Sparse reads will produce zero TPM values for many genes, so the output must not be treated as a production cohort analysis.
